name: GLP-1 cycling / on-off

card.summary: The practice of starting, pausing and restarting GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, discussed by people trying to reach or hold a leaner, more defined look.
card.note: Studies report most lost weight returns within about a year of stopping; discuss any changes with a prescriber.

quick.overview:
GLP-1 cycling describes using GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs, such as semaglutide, in on-and-off periods instead of continuously. People discuss it to reach a leaner body and to manage what happens when the drug stops.
Research cited by Wikipedia reports that people regain roughly half to two thirds of lost weight within a year of stopping these drugs. Studies of formal on-off schedules have not been described.
quick.how: In looksmaxxing and weight-loss communities, people describe a drug phase to lose fat, followed by a break, with lifting and protein intake used to protect muscle. Prescribing decisions belong to clinicians; this entry does not give dosing guidance.
quick.risks: Prescription-only drugs with gastrointestinal side effects. Reported concerns include weight regain after stopping, loss of lean mass in some studies, and cost as a leading reason people stop. Anyone on these drugs should follow their prescriber.

lead: GLP-1 cycling, sometimes called sema cycling after semaglutide, is the pattern of using GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs in on and off periods. People interested in appearance discuss it as a way to lose fat for a leaner, more defined look, and then to hold or reshape that result while the drug is paused.

The drugs themselves reduce appetite and body weight, and the leaner physique and facial definition that follow are the appearance payoff people describe. In the SURMOUNT-4 trial, participants lost a mean of 20.9 percent of body weight on tirzepatide during a 36-week lead-in.[3] Cycling is not a tested regimen: it is a community and consumer pattern layered on top of the drugs, driven partly by cost, side effects and the wish to stop injections.[1][4]

Stopping is common in real-world use. A January 2025 JAMA Network Open study, as summarised by The Healthy, found that 54 percent of people stopped GLP-1 medication within a year and 72.2 percent within two years.[5] A Kantar survey cited by NPR found that most people who quit say they are likely to come back to the drugs.[4] Clinical trials of withdrawal report that much of the lost weight returns, and doctors interviewed by the press describe on-off use as common but not an established protocol.[3][5][6]

chain: Resistance training and protein aim to preserve muscle
angle.text: The drugs themselves reduce weight, producing a leaner appearance. Cycling is a community strategy around stopping and restarting, not a tested regimen. People pair it with strength training and protein to keep the muscle that shapes the physique.

paras: GLP-1 receptor agonists are prescription drugs approved for type 2 diabetes and for weight management. Semaglutide (sold as Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide are the best known. They are taken as weekly injections or, for some products, daily tablets.[2]

Cycling refers to alternating periods of use and non-use rather than continuous therapy. It overlaps with several related patterns that the press and clinicians describe: stopping because of cost or insurance, tapering to a lower maintenance amount, stopping after reaching a target and restarting when weight returns, and so-called microdosing. Of these, only continuous use and abrupt withdrawal have been studied in randomised trials; clinicians interviewed by The Healthy differ on microdosing, with one saying it has not been shown to be effective and another finding it helpful for maintenance once habits are established.[5]

GLP-1 drugs trace to the 1980s-90s work on Gila monster venom. John Eng isolated exendin-4 in 1992, and the synthetic version, exenatide, was approved by the FDA in 2005. Liraglutide followed in 2010 for diabetes and in 2014 for weight management.[1] Semaglutide was approved as Ozempic in the US in 2017 and as higher-dose Wegovy for weight management in June 2021.[2]

The drugs became widely discussed in appearance culture in the early 2020s as influencers and celebrities popularised them for cosmetic and health-related weight loss.[1] The FDA declared shortages of injectable semaglutide and other GLP-1 products in 2022, which allowed compounded versions; Novo Nordisk's chief executive said in January 2026 that up to 1.5 million US users were taking compounded products.[1][2] Analysts quoted by NPR in April 2026 say celebrity use has made on-and-off use seem normal, and that cheaper pills and online sellers that bypass insurance make restarting easier.[4]

Wikipedia summarises studies finding that people regain about half to two thirds of lost weight within a year of stopping this drug class, with return to prior weight in roughly a year and a half.[1] Semaglutide's article cites a 2025 systematic review reporting about 67 percent regained in the following year.[2]

The STEP 1 extension followed 327 participants for 52 weeks after semaglutide and lifestyle support stopped at week 68. Those who had taken semaglutide had lost a mean of 17.3 percent of body weight and regained 11.6 percentage points by week 120, leaving a net loss of 5.6 percent; most cardiometabolic improvements moved back toward baseline. The authors described obesity as chronic and suggested ongoing treatment is needed.[7]

In SURMOUNT-4, 670 participants who had lost weight on tirzepatide were randomised to continue or switch to placebo. Weight changed by -5.5 percent in the continuing group and +14.0 percent in the placebo group over 52 weeks, and 89.5 percent of those continuing kept at least 80 percent of their loss versus 16.6 percent after switching.[3] A post hoc analysis reported that those who stopped mostly regained 25 percent or more of the lost weight and showed greater reversal of cardiometabolic gains.[8]

Real-world data show variety. The Healthy summarises a 2024 Epic Research study of over 20,000 patients in which about 18 percent regained all their weight or more while over half maintained or kept losing.[5]

A 2024 systematic review of six studies, as reported in Wikipedia, found lean mass unchanged in some and reduced by as much as 40 percent of weight lost in others, while the lean-to-total mass ratio rose in all of them.[2] Medical chemist Mahmoud Salama Ahmed told NPR that stopping the drugs often leads to rapid fat regain and that it is unclear how much lost muscle returns, while cardiologist Ian Neeland said muscle quality may improve even as quantity falls.[4]

This is why community and clinical discussion pairs the drugs with resistance training and protein. Dermatologist Doris Day, quoted by Healio in 2026, describes facial volume loss from rapid fat and muscle loss, including temple hollowing and midface deflation, and says the changes resemble those after bariatric surgery; she lists fillers, collagen-stimulating devices and adequate protein among approaches clinicians use.[9] Day also describes hair shedding (telogen effluvium) several months after rapid weight loss.[9]

Nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation are the most common effects; they are dose-related and tend to peak during dose escalation. Gallstones, rare gastroparesis or bowel obstruction, and a possible association with optic neuropathy are reported, and the US label carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours based on rodent data.[1][2] In SURMOUNT-4's double-blind period, nausea occurred in 8.1 percent of tirzepatide recipients versus 2.7 percent on placebo, and serious adverse events were 3.0 percent in both groups.[3]

Doctors quoted by The Healthy say restarting after two or more weeks off can bring stronger gastrointestinal effects and that weight cycling in general has been linked to risks including muscle loss.[5] The drugs are prescription-only; the FDA has warned that some compounded salt forms of semaglutide have not been shown to be safe or effective.[2]

Randomised withdrawal studies exist: the STEP 1 extension of semaglutide and the SURMOUNT-4 trial of tirzepatide both show substantial regain after stopping.[3][7] Observational work describes how often people stop and restart.[4][5] No published trial has tested a planned repeating on-off schedule against continuous use, and researchers quoted in the press say more study of short-term and intermittent use is needed.[4]

timeline.event: John Eng isolates exendin-4 from Gila monster venom, the basis of the first GLP-1 drugs.[1]
Liraglutide is approved for weight management (Saxenda).[1]
Semaglutide approved in the US as Ozempic for diabetes.[2]
Higher-dose semaglutide (Wegovy) approved in the US for weight management.[2]
FDA declares shortages that permit compounding; STEP 1 extension reports weight regain after withdrawal.[1][7]
SURMOUNT-4 published online in December, showing regain after switching tirzepatide to placebo.[3]
Study finds 54 percent stop GLP-1 medication within a year.[5]
NPR reports that many who quit plan to restart; Novo Nordisk puts compounded GLP-1 users at up to 1.5 million.[2][4]

lore.intro: Discussion of stopping and restarting spreads through weight-loss social media, celebrity coverage and online sellers; the claims below are as described in press coverage and clinician interviews.[4][5]

claims.claim: Short courses of GLP-1 drugs can be used to get lean and then stop
claims.believers: Consumers and some sellers frame the drugs as a temporary aid, and NPR reports that celebrity use has normalised this view.[4]
claims.experts: Trials show most lost weight returns within a year of stopping, and clinicians interviewed describe obesity as a chronic condition.[3][4][7]

claims.claim: Tapering or low-amount 'microdosing' maintains results after the main phase
claims.believers: One physician quoted by The Healthy finds a lower maintenance amount helpful once habits are in place.[5]
claims.experts: Another physician says microdosing has not been shown to be effective; no randomised trial has tested it.[5]

claims.claim: Lifting and protein protect muscle during off periods
claims.believers: Clinicians and the community recommend strength training and protein to limit muscle loss.[5][9]
claims.experts: Reviews show lean mass changes vary by study, and it is unclear how much lost muscle returns after fat regain.[2][4]

claims.claim: Facial hollowing from rapid loss can be addressed by gradual loss and fillers
claims.believers: Dermatologists say volume restoration and protein support facial appearance.[9]
claims.experts: Day notes no studies have yet examined facial skin histology on these drugs.[9]

claims.claim: Restarting is easy and low risk
claims.believers: Pills and online sellers lower barriers to restarting, per Kantar's analyst.[4]
claims.experts: Doctors say restarting after a gap can cause stronger gastrointestinal effects, and the FDA has warned about some compounded forms.[2][5]

claims.claim: Weight returns faster after GLP-1s than after diets
claims.believers: Commenters cite regain as a reason to plan for ongoing use.[4]
claims.experts: NPR reports studies suggesting faster regain than after behaviour-change programmes.[4]
